set_evidence: Whenever producer and topic compression do not match, the broker has to compress batches again prior to appending them to the log, which impacts broker performance.

reference:
The CPU goes into recompression. The topic's compression.type (zstd) no longer matches what the producers send (lz4). Whenever producer and topic compression differ, the broker has to compress each batch again before appending it to the log; with 'producer' it keeps the batch as the producer compressed it. At 180 MB/s that puts decompression and zstd compression of all traffic on the produce path, hence CPU and p99.

Fastest way back, no client change:
1. kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --entity-type topics --entity-name clickstream --alter --add-config compression.type=producer
   Do not only --delete-config the topic override: without an override the topic uses the server default, and you also set the cluster-wide broker default to zstd, so recompression would go on.
2. Remove the broker default too, so other topics are not hit: kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --entity-type brokers --entity-default --alter --delete-config compression.type
3. Check with kafka-configs.sh --describe on the topic and on --entity-type brokers --entity-default that nothing resolves to zstd any more, and watch broker CPU and produce latency come down.

If you want zstd on disk later, move the producers to compression.type=zstd (compression.zstd.level if needed) and only then set the topic to zstd or leave it on producer; with matching codecs the broker does not recompress.

Do not try compression.type=uncompressed on the topic: that is another mismatch.
correct_alternative: This is broker-side recompression: the topic and the cluster default say zstd, the producers send lz4, and whenever producer and topic compression differ the broker compresses every batch again before writing it. Since you also want the disk saving, make the codecs match instead of undoing the topic setting: roll the three producer services with compression.type=zstd (compression.zstd.level defaults to 3) and keep the topic on zstd. Once every producer sends zstd the broker stores the batches as they arrive and the CPU and latency return to normal; until the last service is rolled, its lz4 traffic is still recompressed, so roll them back to back. Note that deleting only the topic override would change nothing, because the topic would inherit the cluster-wide default compression.type=zstd. Check with kafka-configs.sh --describe --entity-type topics --entity-name clickstream and watch broker CPU.
generic: High broker CPU after a change usually means the brokers are overloaded. Check the request handler idle ratio and network processor metrics, consider adding brokers or raising num.io.threads and num.network.threads, and review producer batching (linger.ms, batch.size). zstd is a good codec for saving disk; make sure the brokers have enough cores for it.
note: any_of m2a/m2b: either change removes the mismatch; m2a is the quick rollback the question prefers, m2b keeps the disk saving. The recompression fact is stated only in a Strimzi page (con-config-large-messages.adoc) but is about Kafka brokers in general. The kafka-configs describe lines follow ConfigCommand.scala:396-406.

reference:
Nothing is broken on 7 and 8; this is what rack awareness does with an uneven layout. With broker.rack set, Kafka puts the replicas of a partition on as many racks as it can, min(#racks, replication factor) = 3 here, so every partition has one replica in each zone. Zone c has only two brokers to hold its third of all replicas: 1,200 partitions x 3 = 3,600 replicas, 1,200 per zone, so brokers 1-6 carry about 400 replicas each and brokers 7 and 8 about 600 each, 1.5 times as many. That matches 78 % against 52 % and the higher replication bytes in: racks with fewer brokers get more replicas, more storage and more replication.

Leaders are not the issue: the assignment keeps the number of leaders per broker constant whatever the rack layout, which is why the preferred election changed nothing.

Fix: the same number of brokers per rack. Add a ninth broker in zone c with broker.rack set to that zone. A new broker gets no existing partitions on its own, so move replicas onto it with the partition reassignment tool: kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --generate for your topics with --broker-list 1,...,9, review the plan, --execute it with a --throttle, then --verify. Afterwards each broker holds about 400 replicas.

Until then, watch 7 and 8 and lower retention on the biggest topics if they get close to full. Do not remove broker.rack from 7 and 8: you would give up protection against a zone failure.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Brokers 7 and 8 are healthy. Rack-aware assignment places the three replicas of every partition in three different racks, so zone c, with two brokers, must store as many replicas as zones a and b with three brokers each: roughly 600 replicas on each zone-c broker against 400 elsewhere (1,200 partitions, RF 3). Kafka's documentation warns that racks with fewer brokers get more replicas, storage and replication load, and recommends an equal number of brokers per rack. Leadership is spread evenly by the same algorithm, so leader elections will not move disk usage. Plan a ninth broker for zone c; because a newly added broker receives no existing partitions, run a partition reassignment (generate, execute with a throttle, verify) to move replicas onto it. In the meantime, cap growth on 7 and 8 with shorter retention on the largest topics, and keep broker.rack in place.
generic: Uneven disk usage usually comes from skewed partitions or a few large topics. Run a preferred leader election and enable auto.leader.rebalance.enable, look for large partitions with kafka-log-dirs.sh, lower retention.ms on big topics, or add disk to brokers 7 and 8. Cruise Control can also rebalance replicas automatically.
note: One page answers it (basic operations, 'Balancing replicas across racks'). m2 is computed from the question's numbers and not stated in any chunk. Going to 2 brokers per zone would also equalise racks; m4 accepts any equal layout. Distinct from b1-10 (client.rack fetching) and b4-01 (leader order).

reference:
The ACLs are fine; the principal is not what you expect. On an SSL listener with client authentication, Kafka's default principal is the full X.500 distinguished name of the client certificate, here User:CN=orders-app,OU=payments,O=Example,C=DE (ssl.principal.mapping.rules is unset, i.e. DEFAULT). Your ACLs are for User:orders-app, the SCRAM name, so nothing matches and the consumer gets TopicAuthorizationException.

Fix it so the existing ACLs keep working for all thirty services:
1. In server.properties on every broker:
   ssl.principal.mapping.rules=RULE:^CN=(.*?),OU=payments,.*$/$1/,DEFAULT
   (one rule per service OU, or one that matches your service-account naming).
2. The setting is read-only, so roll the brokers one at a time; kafka-configs cannot change it.
3. Rules are evaluated in order and the first match wins; a DN that matches no rule falls through to DEFAULT and keeps its full DN. Keep the rule narrow so that lag-exporter (OU=platform) still maps to its DN and its ACLs keep working. If you prefer a broad CN rule, first add ACLs for the tools' new short names.
4. Restart orders-app; it is now authorized as User:orders-app. Check that Read on its consumer group exists for that name, as it did for SCRAM.

Do not set allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true: orders.events has ACLs, so it would not help, and every topic without ACLs would be open to everyone. Do not add a User:* ACL either.
correct_alternative: No any_of member other than the m4/m4b pair; this answer takes m4b. With mTLS, Kafka names the client after the certificate subject: unless ssl.principal.mapping.rules says otherwise, the principal is the whole DN, User:CN=orders-app,OU=payments,O=Example,C=DE. The ACLs on orders.events are for User:orders-app, so authorization fails although the handshake works. Since thirty services follow, map every certificate to its CN with one rule in each broker's properties, for example ssl.principal.mapping.rules=RULE:^CN=([^,]+),.*$/$1/,DEFAULT. That rule also renames the two monitoring tools (lag-exporter becomes User:lag-exporter), so before the change add ACLs for their new short names with kafka-acls.sh --add, mirroring their current DN ACLs. The property is read-only, so the brokers have to be restarted, one at a time, before the rule applies; then restart the consumer. allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found does not apply to a topic that has ACLs and would open every topic without ACLs, so leave it false.
generic: TopicAuthorizationException means the client is not allowed to read the topic. Check that the ACLs exist with kafka-acls.sh --list, make sure the consumer also has Read on its group, verify the keystore and truststore paths and passwords, and check that ssl.client.auth is set correctly on the listener. Restart the consumer after fixing the permissions.
note: Second review: m4/m4b any_of (narrow rule with DEFAULT last, or broad rule plus new ACLs for the tools); m3 reworded to what the chunks state (read-only, restart). No any_of for m2: adding ACLs for each DN principal is correct for one service but does not keep the existing name-based ACLs working for thirty services, which is what the question asks ('fix it properly'); the reference mentions DN ACLs only for the monitoring tools. The keytool line is an invented value in keytool's 'Owner:' format; Kafka shows the DN without spaces (RFC 2253). reference:
Step 1 would destroy the archive: to set remote.storage.enable=false you must also set remote.log.delete.on.disable=true, and that deletes the topic's tiered data. Step 2 before the topic is off makes the brokers fail at startup.

Sequence:
1. Monday, stop uploads but keep the remote data readable:
   kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name audit-archive --add-config 'remote.storage.enable=true,remote.log.copy.disable=true,local.retention.ms=-2,local.retention.bytes=-2'
   With copying disabled, local retention no longer applies, so set the local limits to -2 (or equal to retention.ms/retention.bytes).
2. Check the disks first. From then on new data expires only by retention.ms (180 days) and stays on local disk: 2 TB a month x RF 3 is about 6 TB a month across 6 brokers, about 1 TB per broker per month, against about 2.9 TB free. That lasts about three months. Lower retention.ms for audit-archive (it also ages out the remote copy sooner), add disk, or accept that new data lives shorter.
3. When the last remote segment has expired (about 180 days after the stop at the current retention), switch the topic off: remote.storage.enable=false,remote.log.delete.on.disable=true (nothing is left to delete).
4. Only then the cluster level. The docs say topics that used tiered storage must be deleted before remote.log.storage.system.enable=false; plan to move audit-archive's data into a new topic if you need it, then delete the topic, set the broker property, remove the plugin and roll the brokers.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Do not set remote.storage.enable=false yet: disabling tiered storage on a topic requires remote.log.delete.on.disable=true, which removes everything already in the bucket. To freeze the bucket while keeping it readable, set remote.log.copy.disable=true on audit-archive and leave remote.storage.enable=true; the remote segments become read-only. Set local.retention.ms=-2 and local.retention.bytes=-2 at the same time, since local retention stops applying. Expect all new data to stay on the brokers until the 180-day retention.ms: at about 6 TB a month of replicated data across six brokers, the free space of roughly 2.9 TB each runs out in about three months, so shorten retention.ms or add disk. Turn the topic off with remote.log.delete.on.disable=true only when the remote data has expired, and set remote.log.storage.system.enable=false last: the docs require the tiered topics to be deleted first, and brokers that still have one fail to start.
generic: Tiered storage can be turned off per topic with remote.storage.enable and per broker with remote.log.storage.system.enable. Test the change in staging first, make sure the plugin is removed cleanly, and monitor disk usage on the brokers after the change. Keep a backup of the bucket until you are sure the data is no longer needed.

Do not touch the topic itself; move each partition's log start offset past the last bad record. DeleteRecords does exactly that and drops the old segments.

```python
from confluent_kafka import TopicPartition
from confluent_kafka.admin import AdminClient, OffsetSpec

TOPIC = "audit-trail"
CUTOFF_MS = 1795168800000  # 2026-11-20T10:00:00Z
admin = AdminClient(conf)  # svc-purge's SASL/SSL settings

parts = admin.list_topics(TOPIC, timeout=10).topics[TOPIC].partitions
query = {TopicPartition(TOPIC, p): OffsetSpec.for_timestamp(CUTOFF_MS) for p in parts}
cut = []
for tp, fut in admin.list_offsets(query).items():
    off = fut.result().offset
    if off < 0:
        print(f"partition {tp.partition}: no offset returned, check by hand")
        continue
    cut.append(TopicPartition(TOPIC, tp.partition, off))

for tp, fut in admin.delete_records(cut).items():
    print(f"partition {tp.partition}: log start now {fut.result().low_watermark}")
```

- A group whose committed offset is now below the log start offset gets its auto.offset.reset policy: latest would skip to the end. Check the three groups (kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe) and use earliest.
- Copies elsewhere (mirrors, sinks, backups) are not affected.

reference:
The handshake fails on host name verification. The Java client checks the name it connected to, kafka-core.corp.example.net, against the subject alternative names of the certificate. The certificates come from the Strimzi cluster CA and list only the service and load balancer names; a DNS CNAME does not change them. With the old load balancer name the check passes, which is why that still works.

Add the alias to the listener:

listeners:
  - name: external
    port: 9094
    type: loadbalancer
    tls: true
    authentication:
      type: scram-sha-512
    configuration:
      bootstrap:
        alternativeNames:
          - kafka-core.corp.example.net

The names in alternativeNames are added to the broker certificates and can be used for TLS hostname verification. Only the bootstrap name is needed: bootstrap.servers is used only for the initial connection, then the clients discover the brokers and connect to their own advertised addresses, which are already in the certificates.

Timing: this is a user-driven change that changes the SANs, so the operator renews the certificates and rolls the brokers when you apply it. The Sunday window does not delay it. Apply it at a quiet time and watch the roll.

Do not empty ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm. The Strimzi docs show that only for nodeport listeners, and it turns off the check that protects the SCRAM credentials.
correct_alternative: No alternative path is documented; the fix is the same, worded differently. The error means the certificate presented on 9094 has no SAN entry for kafka-core.corp.example.net. Clients verify the name they connect to, and the CNAME you added only exists in DNS. Set spec.kafka.listeners[external].configuration.bootstrap.alternativeNames: [kafka-core.corp.example.net]; Strimzi adds the names to the TLS certificates' SAN list. Only the bootstrap address needs it, because clients use bootstrap.servers only for the first connection and then talk to the brokers at the addresses they advertise. The roll that follows is not held for the maintenance window: a change you make to the Kafka resource that changes SANs rolls straight away. Keep hostname verification on in the clients.

Use openssl s_client to inspect the certificate chain. Make sure DNS resolves correctly and plan certificate changes in a maintenance window.

    + " oauth.ssl.truststore.location=\"/etc/pki/corp-ca.p12\""
    + " oauth.ssl.truststore.password=\"" + System.getenv("CORP_CA_PASSWORD") + "\""

import os
from confluent_kafka import Consumer

CERTS = ["/etc/kafka/certs/ca.crt", "/etc/kafka/certs/user.crt", "/etc/kafka/certs/user.key"]
CONF = {
    "bootstrap.servers": "kafka-core.corp.example.net:9094",
    "security.protocol": "SSL",
    "ssl.ca.location": CERTS[0],           # from core-cluster-ca-cert
    "ssl.certificate.location": CERTS[1],  # from Secret meter-reader
    "ssl.key.location": CERTS[2],
    "group.id": "meter-reader",
    "enable.auto.commit": False,
    "auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
}

def stamp():
    return tuple(os.stat(p).st_mtime_ns for p in CERTS)

def start():
    c = Consumer(CONF)
    c.subscribe(["meter-readings"])
    return c

seen = stamp()
consumer = start()
while True:
    msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
    if msg is not None and not msg.error():
        store(msg)
        consumer.commit(message=msg, asynchronous=False)
    if stamp() != seen:          # renewed files, including ca.crt
        consumer.close()         # leaves the group; offsets already committed
        seen = stamp()
        consumer = start()       # loads the new files, resumes from commits

Each record is committed synchronously after store(), so the new consumer starts after the last stored record. Nothing is lost or skipped. Keep certificate verification on.

import json, sys, urllib.parse, urllib.request
API = "http://etl-connect-api.data.svc:8083"   # in-cluster service <connect>-connect-api:8083

def validate(kc):
    spec = kc["spec"]
    cfg = {k: str(v) for k, v in spec.get("config", {}).items()}
    cfg["connector.class"] = spec["class"]
    cfg["tasks.max"] = str(spec.get("tasksMax", 1))
    cfg["name"] = kc["metadata"]["name"]
    plugin = urllib.parse.quote(spec["class"], safe="")
    req = urllib.request.Request(f"{API}/connector-plugins/{plugin}/config/validate",
        method="PUT", data=json.dumps(cfg).encode(),

3. Do not roll the cluster back and do not restart the producers: they need no restart. If you ever want the old behaviour, the transactional protocol can be downgraded safely and clients switch on their next transaction.

The clean-up changed the join's semantics, not just its spelling. JoinWindows.of(...).grace(...) kept the old eager behaviour: a left join emitted [order, null] at once when no payment was there yet, hence the alerts for orders paid a minute later. The new builders (ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace, ofTimeDifferenceWithNoGrace) enable the KIP-633 fix: left results are emitted only after the join window is closed, after the grace period. Your window ends 30 minutes after the order and the grace adds 2 hours, so the alert comes about 2 h 30 min later.

The overnight cases come from stream time. The grace is measured in stream time, which advances only when new records arrive; with no orders or payments at night, nothing closes the window until morning traffic moves stream time on.

Fix:
1. Keep the new builder and set the grace to the lateness you must tolerate, e.g. JoinWindows.ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(30), Duration.ofMinutes(5)); alerts then come about 35 minutes after the order. With ofTimeDifferenceWithNoGrace they come right after 30 minutes.
2. Know the trade-off: a payment later than window end plus grace is dropped, so those rare two-hour-late payments will produce an alert for a paid order; handle them downstream (the payments team can close the alert).
3. Expect quiet periods to delay alerts until the next record arrives.

Do not go back to JoinWindows.of(): that brings the false alerts back.

Grace is counted in stream time, driven by record timestamps, so during the night, with no new orders or payments, the windows close only when the first records of the morning arrive. Shorten the grace instead of reverting: ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(30), Duration.ofMinutes(10)) gives alerts about 40 minutes after the order. A payment later than that is dropped as late, so the paged team will occasionally see an alert for an order that was paid after all.
